cards.explanation: The answer is that Elijah wants them to decide who is God and follow. Elijah, the LORD's prophet, puts it plain: “If the LORD is God, follow Him. But if Baal is God, follow him.” (1 Kings 18:21) Baal is a false god. So he isn't asking for a mood or a maybe, friends. He's asking for a choice, and then for following.
The answer is False. After Elijah's challenge, “…the people did not answer a word.” (1 Kings 18:21) Not a shout, not a whisper. Picture a whole crowd on a mountain and not one of them says a thing.

The answer is that each side will call on the name of its god. Elijah says, “Then you may call on the name of your god, and I will call on the name of the LORD.” (1 Kings 18:24) Both bulls are on the wood with no fire lit, so each side calls on its god. The one who answers settles it.
The answer is fire. Elijah says, “The God who answers by fire, He is God.” (1 Kings 18:24) Both bulls sit on the wood with nothing lit. So whoever sends the flame has answered.
The answer is True. After Elijah lays out the plan, the people answered, “What you say is good.” (1 Kings 18:24) Remember, they'd said nothing a moment before. Now they're on board.

The answer is True. Elijah says to the prophets of Baal, “Since you are so numerous, choose for yourselves one bull and prepare it first.” (1 Kings 18:25) They have four hundred and fifty prophets to his one, so they go first. Then he adds, “…do not light the fire.”

The answer is no sound at all. Silence. The text says, “But there was no sound, and no one answered as they leaped around the altar they had made.” (1 Kings 18:26) They shouted from morning until noon. All that effort, and no one answered.

The answer is True. Elijah says, “Perhaps he is deep in thought, or occupied, or on a journey. Perhaps he is sleeping and must be awakened!” (1 Kings 18:27) He's taunting the prophets of Baal. That's a whole list of excuses, friends, and I've used a few of them on my own snooze button.

The answer is False. The text says, “So they shouted louder and cut themselves with knives and lances, as was their custom, until the blood gushed over them.” (1 Kings 18:28) This part is heavy. Instead of going quiet, they kept at it.

The answer is until the evening sacrifice. The text says, “Midday passed, and they kept on raving until the time of the evening sacrifice.” (1 Kings 18:29) They started in the morning, so that's a long day of calling. And the verse ends, “…there was no response; no one answered, no one paid attention.”

The answer is that he repairs it. The text says he “…repaired the altar of the LORD that had been torn down.” (1 Kings 18:30) The altar was torn down, and Elijah is the one who repaired it. He does it right after telling the people, “Come near to me.”

The answer is one for each tribe of Jacob's sons. That's the reason the text gives. Elijah took twelve stones, “…one for each tribe of the sons of Jacob…” (1 Kings 18:31) These are the tribes the word of the LORD came to, saying Israel would be their name. Twelve tribes, twelve stones.

The answer is water, friends. Elijah says, “Fill four waterpots and pour the water on the offering and on the wood.” (1 Kings 18:34) That's water on a bull and wood that are already on the altar. I've never seen a baker do that, and I've seen plenty.

The answer is True. Elijah says, “Fill four waterpots and pour the water on the offering and on the wood.” Then, “Do it a second time…” and “Do it a third time…” (1 Kings 18:34) That's three rounds, and the text says they did it each time.

The answer is that He is God in Israel. That's the heart of Elijah's prayer. He says, “O LORD, God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, let it be known this day that You are God in Israel and that I am Your servant and have done all these things at Your command.” (1 Kings 18:36) He prays for the LORD to be known, and he calls himself the LORD's servant.

The answer is True. Elijah prays, “Answer me, O LORD! Answer me, so that this people will know that You, the LORD, are God, and that You have turned their hearts back again.” (1 Kings 18:37) He asks twice for an answer. And he asks for it so the people will know.

The answer is False. The text says, “Then the fire of the LORD fell and consumed the sacrifice, the wood, the stones, and the dust, and it licked up the water in the trench.” (1 Kings 18:38) It took the sacrifice, the wood, the stones, the dust and the water. Nothing was left out.

The answer is that they fall facedown and say the LORD is God. After the fire of the LORD fell, “When all the people saw this, they fell facedown and said, ‘The LORD, He is God! The LORD, He is God!’” (1 Kings 18:39) Earlier on that mountain they did not answer Elijah a word. Now they say it twice.

The answer is False. Elijah orders, “Seize the prophets of Baal! Do not let a single one escape.” Then the text says, “So they seized them…” (1 Kings 18:40) This part is heavy. The order was followed.

The answer is a heavy rain. Elijah says to Ahab, king of Israel, “Go up, eat and drink, for there is the sound of a heavy rain.” (1 Kings 18:41) He says it before the servant reports any cloud. Elijah is already talking about the sound of rain.

The answer is that he bends down with his face between his knees. The text says Elijah “…climbed to the summit of Carmel, bent down on the ground, and put his face between his knees.” (1 Kings 18:42) Ahab heads off to eat and drink. Elijah goes up and bends low.
The answer is True. The servant says, “There is nothing there.” and the text says, “Seven times Elijah said, ‘Go back.’” (1 Kings 18:43) Nothing there is not the last word. The servant goes again.

The answer is a cloud. On the seventh time the servant reports, “There is a cloud as small as a man’s hand rising from the sea.” (1 Kings 18:44) That's a cloud about the size of a hand. Seven times Elijah said, “Go back.” before he got that report.

The answer is to get your chariot and go before the rain stops you. Elijah says, “Go and tell Ahab, ‘Prepare your chariot and go down before the rain stops you.’” (1 Kings 18:44) Ahab is the king of Israel. A cloud as small as a hand, and Elijah already has a message about the rain.

The answer is Jezreel. The text says, “So Ahab rode away and went to Jezreel.” (1 Kings 18:45) The sky had gone dark with clouds and wind, and heavy rain was falling. The king of Israel is off in his chariot.

The answer is False. The text says, “…the hand of the LORD came upon Elijah, and he tucked his cloak into his belt and ran ahead of Ahab all the way to Jezreel.” (1 Kings 18:46) Ahab rode away in his chariot. Elijah ran ahead of him on his own two feet.
